fields.title: Micah
fields.subtitle: Mikhah, “Who is like the LORD?”
fields.description: The words of a countryman from Moresheth who spoke for the farmers and villagers of Judah in the days of Isaiah, when Assyria swept through the land. Micah denounces those who covet fields and seize them, rulers who devour the people, and prophets who cry “Peace!” for pay; he warns that Zion will be plowed as a field; and he sees the nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD, swords hammered into plow blades, everyone under their own vine and fig tree. From little Bethlehem a ruler will come, and he will be our peace. Then the great question, “what does the LORD ask of you?”, and the hymn that ends the book: “Who is a God like you?” Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Micah?
qa.answer: The sixth of the twelve shorter prophetic books of the Old Testament. Its seven chapters fall into three movements, each opening with a call to listen (1:2, 3:1, 6:1) and each moving from judgment to hope: against Samaria and Jerusalem and the land-grabbers of Judah (1–2); against corrupt rulers and prophets, with visions of the nations coming to Zion and a ruler from Bethlehem (3–5); and God’s case against his people, ending with a hymn to the God who forgives (6–7).

qa.question: Who was Micah, and when did he prophesy?
qa.answer: Micah of Moresheth, a small town in the low hills of south-west Judah, who prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (1:1), roughly 740–700 BC. He was a younger contemporary of Isaiah, and his years of ministry saw the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and the Assyrian invasion of Judah in 701 BC. A century later the elders of Judah quoted his warning that “Zion will be plowed as a field” in defence of Jeremiah, and recalled that King Hezekiah had listened to it (Jeremiah 26:18–19). His name is a shortened form of Micaiah, which means “Who is like the LORD?”

qa.question: What does Micah 6:8 mean?
qa.answer: It answers the question of what a person can bring to God. The people ask whether God wants burnt offerings, thousands of rams, rivers of oil, even their firstborn; Micah replies, “He has told you, mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?” To do justice is to treat others rightly, especially the weak; to love loyalty (Hebrew hesed, often translated “mercy”) is to cherish faithful, covenant love; and to walk humbly with God is to live every day in his company and under his direction.

qa.question: Does Micah say the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem?
qa.answer: Micah 5:2 promises that from Bethlehem Ephrathah, the small town of David’s family, “one will come out for me to be ruler over Israel, one whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.” By the time of Jesus it was understood as a prophecy of the Messiah: when Herod asked where the Christ would be born, the chief priests and scribes answered “In Bethlehem in Judea” and quoted this verse (Matthew 2:5–6). Christians read it as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus, and many hear in “from of old, from ancient days” a hint of his eternal origin.

qa.question: Why are Micah 4:1–3 and Isaiah 2:2–4 almost the same?
qa.answer: Both prophets give, nearly word for word, the vision of the mountain of the LORD raised above all others, with the nations streaming to it to learn his ways and hammering their swords into plow blades. Micah and Isaiah were contemporaries, and scholars differ on whether one prophet took the oracle from the other or both drew on an older prophecy or temple song. Micah adds a line of his own: “Everyone will sit under their own vine and under their own fig tree, with no one to frighten them” (4:4).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
He has told you, mortal, what is good. And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God?

— Micah 6:8

Micah was a countryman. He came from Moresheth, a small town in the low hills of Judah’s south-west, the farming country between the mountains and the coastal plain, and he spoke for the people of such places: farmers losing their fields to rich men from the city, families driven out of their homes, villagers who saw the soldiers of every invading army pass by first. His book is angry, and it is full of hope, and it contains what may be the best-known summary of what God wants from human beings in the whole Old Testament.

His name is a question. Micah is a shortened form of Micaiah, which means “Who is like the LORD?”, and the book ends by asking it of God himself: “Who is a God like you, who forgives wrongdoing and passes over rebellion for the remnant of his inheritance?”

The prophet of Moresheth

The first verse places Micah in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, roughly from 740 to 700 BC. He was a younger contemporary of Isaiah, and the two prophets share a vision of the nations coming to Zion that appears in both their books almost word for word. Isaiah moved among kings in Jerusalem; Micah looked at Jerusalem from the countryside, and he did not like what he saw.

These were the decades of Assyria’s great advance. Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, fell in 722 BC, and in 701 the Assyrian king Sennacherib swept through Judah, taking its fortified towns one by one, among them Lachish, a few miles from Micah’s home, before laying siege to Jerusalem. Micah’s book opens with God coming down to tread on the heights of the earth, mountains melting beneath him, because of the sins of both capitals:

All this is because of Jacob’s rebellion and because of the sins of the house of Israel. What is Jacob’s rebellion? Is it not Samaria? And what are Judah’s high places? Are they not Jerusalem?

— Micah 1:5

Then Micah walks the reader through the towns of his own district, a lament built out of puns that are mostly lost in translation. “Do not tell it in Gath”, he begins, echoing David’s lament for Saul; in Beth-leaphrah, “house of dust”, they are to roll in the dust; Lachish, the great fortress of the region, is told to harness the horses to the chariot. The disaster that struck Samaria “has reached the gate of my people, Jerusalem itself.”

Three times, from judgment to hope

The book is built in three movements, each beginning with a summons to listen: “Listen, all you peoples” (1:2), “Listen, you leaders of Jacob” (3:1), and “Listen to what the LORD says” (6:1). Each moves from judgment to hope. Chapters 1–2 end with God gathering a remnant like sheep in a pen; chapters 3–5 with a ruler from Bethlehem; chapters 6–7 with a God who throws sins into the sea.

Those who covet fields

Micah’s first target is the land-grabbers:

Woe to those who plot wickedness and lie on their beds working out evil! When morning dawns they carry it out, because they have the power to do it. They covet fields and seize them, houses, and take them away. They crush a man and his household, a man and his inheritance.

— Micah 2:1–2

In Israel the land was God’s gift, divided among families as their inheritance, never to be sold away for good. To seize a family’s fields was to rob it of its place among God’s people. So Micah tells the grabbers that God will take their fields too, and that they will have no one left to stretch out a measuring line for them “in the assembly of the LORD.”

His hearers did not want to hear it. “Stop preaching,” they preach. “No one should preach about such things.” Micah answers with a bitter joke: if someone came along, full of wind and lies, and promised to preach about wine and beer, “he would be just the preacher for this people!”

Leaders who devour

Chapter 3 turns on the leaders of Jacob, the very people who should have known what justice is. Micah’s language is shocking on purpose. They “tear the skin off my people and the flesh off their bones”, chop them up “like meat for the pot”. He turns next to the prophets, who cry “Peace!” to anyone who feeds them, and to the priests and judges who work for pay. Yet they all lean on the LORD and say, “Is not the LORD among us? No disaster will come upon us.” Against them Micah sets his own calling:

But I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, with justice and strength, to tell Jacob of his rebellion and Israel of his sin.

— Micah 3:8

And then comes a sentence no prophet before him had spoken so bluntly against Zion and its temple: “Zion will be plowed as a field, Jerusalem will be a mound of ruins”. It was remembered. A century later, when Jeremiah was on trial for his life for predicting the temple’s fall, some of the elders quoted Micah’s words in his defence. King Hezekiah, they said, had not put Micah to death; he had feared the LORD and sought his favour, and the LORD had relented.

The mountain of the LORD

Immediately after the ruined temple mount, Micah sees the same mountain raised high above all others, and the nations streaming to it:

Nations in great numbers will set out, saying, “Come, let us climb to the mountain of the LORD, up to the house of Jacob’s God, so that he may show us his ways and we may walk on his paths.” For instruction will go out from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem. He will be judge between many peoples and settle the cases of mighty nations far away. They will hammer their swords into plow blades and their spears into knives for pruning. No nation will raise the sword against another, and they will no longer learn how to wage war.

— Micah 4:2–3

The same vision stands at the beginning of Isaiah. Whether one prophet took it from the other, or both drew on a psalm sung in the temple, it was clearly treasured. Micah adds a line of his own, the countryman’s picture of peace: “Everyone will sit under their own vine and under their own fig tree, with no one to frighten them”. It is the opposite of chapter 2, where the powerful seized the fields of the poor. In God’s kingdom every family is home, and safe.

The rest of chapter 4 holds hope and pain together. God will gather “those who limp” and make them a strong nation. Daughter Zion must first writhe like a woman in labor and go to Babylon, but “There the LORD will redeem you”. It is striking that a prophet of Micah’s time, when Assyria was the great power, names Babylon as the place of exile and rescue. Some scholars think the line was added after the exile; others note that Babylon was already courting Hezekiah in Micah’s day, as the second book of Kings records.

Bethlehem

Then, out of a city under siege and a ruler struck on the cheek, comes one of the great promises of the Old Testament:

But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, too small to be counted among the clans of Judah, from you one will come out for me to be ruler over Israel, one whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.

— Micah 5:2

Bethlehem was David’s town, small and unimpressive. Micah says that God will begin again where he began with David, not in the palace but in the village. The coming ruler will “shepherd his flock by the power of the LORD”, his greatness will reach to the ends of the earth, “And he will be our peace.” Centuries later, when wise men from the east came to Jerusalem asking where the king of the Jews had been born, the chief priests and scribes turned to this verse and answered, “In Bethlehem in Judea”.

The phrase about his origins, “from of old, from ancient days”, has been read in two ways: as pointing back to the ancient line of David, or, as many Christians have read it, to a ruler whose goings forth are from eternity. The chapter goes on to promise that the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations “like dew sent by the LORD”, and that God will cut off from his people every horse and chariot, every idol and sorcery they trusted instead of him.

What does the LORD ask?

The last movement opens in a courtroom. God calls the mountains to be the jury and brings his case against his people. But the charge is a lament:

My people, what have I done to you? How have I made you weary? Testify against me! For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt; I redeemed you from the house where you were slaves. I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam to lead you.

— Micah 6:3–4

These words became the heart of the Reproaches, the ancient Good Friday chant in which Christ speaks from the cross: “My people, what have I done to you?”

The people answer with a frantic question. What can they bring? Burnt offerings, year-old calves, thousands of rams, ten thousand streams of olive oil, even their firstborn child? And the prophet answers with the verse at the head of this introduction. God has already told them. Justice, loyalty, and a humble walk with God: none of these can be bought, and all of them can be practised by anyone, in any village, every day.

“Who is a God like you?”

The final chapter begins in desolation. Micah looks for one upright person and finds none, “like one who comes when the summer fruit is gathered” and finds no grapes left. Trust has collapsed even in the home: “a person’s enemies are the people of their own household.” Jesus quoted those words when he warned his disciples of what following him might cost.

Then the prophet turns, and speaks for his people as one of them:

But I will keep watch for the LORD; I will put my hope in the God who saves me; my God will hear me. Do not gloat over me, my enemy! I have fallen, but I will rise. Though I sit in darkness, the LORD is my light.

— Micah 7:7–8

And the book closes with a hymn on Micah’s own name:

Who is a God like you, who forgives wrongdoing and passes over rebellion for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not keep his anger forever, because he delights in loyal love. He will again show us compassion and trample our wrongdoings underfoot. You will hurl all their sins into the depths of the sea.

— Micah 7:18–19

These verses have a long life in worship. Jews read them on the Day of Atonement, after the book of Jonah, and recite them at the New Year beside running water, in a custom called Tashlikh, “you will hurl”, after the verb in verse 19. Christians have found in them one of the clearest pictures of forgiveness: sins not merely covered but thrown into the depths of the sea.

How to read Micah

Read it in its three movements, 1–2, 3–5 and 6–7, and watch each turn from judgment to hope. Keep the setting in mind: a small country caught between empires, its villages plundered from outside and its poor exploited from within. Notice how concrete Micah’s sins are, fields and houses, bribes and false weights, and how concrete his hopes, a vine and a fig tree, a shepherd, a village. Some scholars think the book’s hopeful passages were added by later hands; others see the alternation of doom and hope as the prophet’s own design. Either way, the book as it stands insists that judgment is never God’s last word.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Most of Micah is poetry, and this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation writes “the LORD”, and where it joins that name to the word for “Lord”, “the Lord GOD” (1:2). The title older Bibles render “the LORD of hosts” is “the LORD of Armies” (4:4).

Loyalty and loyal love. The Hebrew hesed, which older Bibles render “mercy”, is “loyal love” in the closing hymn (“he delights in loyal love”) and “loyalty” in 6:8, where God asks us “to love loyalty”. In the same verse the Hebrew adam, “human being”, is rendered “mortal”: “He has told you, mortal, what is good.”

Numbering. The Hebrew counts the first verse of English chapter 5 as the last verse of chapter 4, so the promise about Bethlehem is 5:1 in Hebrew and 5:2 in English. This edition follows the English chapters, and the references in it follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Micah 1
fields.body_html:
The LORD comes against Samaria and Jerusalem

The LORD’s word came to Micah of Moresheth during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah. It is what he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
Listen, all you peoples;
pay attention, earth and everything in it!
Let the Lord GOD be a witness against you,
the Lord from his holy temple.
See, the LORD is coming out from his dwelling;
he will come down and tread on the heights of the earth.
The mountains will melt beneath him,
and the valleys will burst apart,
like wax before the fire,
like water rushing down a steep slope.
All this is because of Jacob’s rebellion
and because of the sins of the house of Israel.
What is Jacob’s rebellion? Is it not Samaria?
And what are Judah’s high places?
Are they not Jerusalem?
So I will make Samaria a heap of rubble in the open country, a place for planting vineyards.
I will hurl her stones down into the valley
and lay her foundations bare.
All her carved idols will be smashed to pieces, all her temple gifts burned in the fire,
and I will lay waste all her images.
For she collected them from a prostitute’s pay,
and they will go back to be a prostitute’s pay.
For this I will mourn and wail;
I will go about barefoot and stripped.
I will howl like the jackals
and mourn like the ostriches.
For her wound cannot be healed;
it has spread to Judah.
It has reached the gate of my people, Jerusalem itself.
Do not tell it in Gath;
do not weep at all.
In Beth-leaphrah, roll in the dust.
Pass on your way, people of Shaphir, in shameful nakedness.
The people of Zaanan have not come out.
Beth-ezel is mourning;
it will take its support away from you.
The people of Maroth writhe in pain as they wait for relief,
for disaster has come down from the LORD
to the very gate of Jerusalem.
Harness the horses to the chariot, people of Lachish!
You were the beginning of sin for Daughter Zion,
for the rebellious ways of Israel were found in you.
So you will give farewell gifts
to Moresheth-gath.
The houses of Achzib will prove a deception
to the kings of Israel.
I will once more bring a conqueror against you,
people of Mareshah.
The glory of Israel will come to Adullam.
Shave your head in mourning
for the children you delight in.
Make yourself as bald as the vulture,
for they will be taken from you into exile.

fields.title: Micah 2
fields.body_html:
Woe to those who plan evil

Woe to those who plot wickedness and lie on their beds working out evil!
When morning dawns they carry it out,
because they have the power to do it.
They covet fields and seize them,
houses, and take them away.
They crush a man and his household,
a man and his inheritance.

The LORD plans disaster against this clan

Therefore the LORD says this:
See, I am planning disaster against this clan,
a yoke you cannot free your necks from; you will no longer walk proudly,
for it will be a time of disaster.
On that day people will sing a taunt song about you and wail in bitter lament, “We are completely ruined!
He hands over my people’s share to others.
How he takes it away from me!
He parcels out our fields to a traitor.”
So you will have no one
to stretch out a measuring line by lot
in the assembly of the LORD.
“Stop preaching,” they preach.
“No one should preach about such things.
Disgrace will not catch up with us.”
Should this be said, house of Jacob? “Has the LORD run out of patience?
Are these the things he does?”
Do my words not do good
to the one whose life is upright?
But lately my people have risen up like an enemy.
You strip the cloak off the tunic
of those who pass by without a care,
people who want nothing to do with war.
You drive the women of my people
out of the homes they love;
from their young children
you take away my glory forever.
Get up and go!
This is not the place of rest,
because uncleanness brings destruction, a painful destruction.
If someone came along, full of wind and lies, saying,
“I will preach to you
about wine and beer,”
he would be just the preacher for this people!
I will gather all of you, Jacob; I will surely bring together the remnant of Israel.
I will put them together like sheep in a pen,
like a flock in its pasture;
the place will be loud with people.
The one who breaks through will go up ahead of them;
they will break out, go through the gate,
and leave by it.
Their king will go on before them,
the LORD at their head.

fields.title: Micah 3
fields.body_html:
Rulers who hate good

And I said: Listen, you leaders of Jacob,
you rulers of Israel’s house!
Should you not know what justice is?
You who hate good and love evil,
who tear the skin off my people
and the flesh off their bones,
who eat the flesh of my people,
strip off their skin,
break their bones,
and chop them up like meat for the pot,
like flesh in a cooking kettle.
Then they will call to the LORD for help,
but he will give them no answer.
When that time comes he will hide his face from them,
for their deeds have been evil.

Prophets who lead the people astray

The LORD says this
about the prophets who lead my people astray,
who cry, “Peace!” when they have something to bite with their teeth,
but against anyone who puts nothing into their mouths
they declare a holy war.
Therefore night will come on you, with no vision,
and darkness, with no divination.
The sun will set on the prophets,
and the day will turn black over them.
The seers will be put to shame and the diviners disgraced;
they will all cover their faces,
because there is no answer from God.
But I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD,
with justice and strength,
to tell Jacob of his rebellion
and Israel of his sin.

Zion will be plowed as a field

Listen to this, you leaders of the house of Jacob,
you rulers of the house of Israel,
who hate justice
and twist everything that is right,
who build Zion with bloodshed
and Jerusalem with wrongdoing.
Her leaders give judgment for a bribe, her priests teach for pay,
and her prophets tell fortunes for money.
Yet they lean on the LORD and say,
“Is not the LORD among us?
No disaster will come upon us.”
Therefore, because of you,
Zion will be plowed as a field,
Jerusalem will be a mound of ruins,
and the mountain of the temple a wooded height.

fields.title: Micah 4
fields.body_html:
The mountain of the LORD’s house

In days to come, the mountain of the LORD’s house will stand firm, the chief of all the mountains,
rising high above the hills,
and peoples will stream toward it.
Nations in great numbers will set out, saying, “Come, let us climb to the mountain of the LORD, up to the house of Jacob’s God,
so that he may show us his ways and we may walk on his paths.”
For instruction will go out from Zion,
and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
He will be judge between many peoples
and settle the cases of mighty nations far away.
They will hammer their swords into plow blades and their spears into knives for pruning.
No nation will raise the sword against another,
and they will no longer learn how to wage war.
Everyone will sit under their own vine and under their own fig tree, with no one to frighten them,
for the mouth of the LORD of Armies has spoken.
All the peoples may walk,
each in the name of its own god,
but we will walk in the name of our God, the LORD, for all time to come.

The LORD will gather the lame

On that day, declares the LORD, I will gather those who limp;
I will bring together the scattered,
those I have brought harm on.
I will make the lame into a remnant
and those driven far off into a strong nation,
and the LORD will reign over them on Mount Zion
from now on and forever.

The former rule will return

And you, watchtower of the flock, stronghold of Daughter Zion, to you it will come:
the former rule will return,
the kingdom of Daughter Jerusalem.
Now, why do you cry out so loudly?
Is there no king among you? Has your adviser died,
that pain grips you like a woman in labor?
Writhe and groan, Daughter Zion, like a woman in labor,
for now you must leave the city and camp in the open country. You will go to Babylon, and there you will find rescue.
There the LORD will redeem you
from the grasp of your enemies.
But now many nations are gathered against you.
They say, “Let her be profaned,
and let our eyes gloat over Zion!”
But they do not know what the LORD has in mind;
they do not understand his plan,
that he has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor.
Rise up and thresh, Daughter Zion, for I will give you horns of iron and hoofs of bronze,
and you will crush many peoples.
You will devote their plunder to the LORD,
their wealth to the Lord of the whole earth.

fields.title: Micah 5
fields.body_html:
A ruler from Bethlehem

Now gash yourself in grief, daughter of raiders;
a siege has been laid against us.
With a rod they strike the ruler of Israel
on the cheek.

But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, too small to be counted among the clans of Judah,
from you one will come out for me
to be ruler over Israel,
one whose origins are from of old, from ancient days.
So he will abandon them
until the woman in labor has borne her child;
then the rest of his kinsmen will come back
to the people of Israel.
He will stand firm and shepherd his flock by the power of the LORD,
by the majesty of the name of the LORD his God.
His people will live in safety,
for then his greatness will reach to the ends of the earth.
And he will be our peace.
When the Assyrians invade our land and march into our strongholds,
we will raise up seven shepherds against it,
eight leaders of the people.
They will rule the land of Assyria with the sword,
the land of Nimrod at its gates.
He will rescue us from Assyria
when it invades our land
and marches across our borders.

The remnant of Jacob among the nations

The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples
like dew sent by the LORD,
like showers on the grass,
which wait for no one
and depend on no human being.
The remnant of Jacob will live among the nations, surrounded by many peoples,
like a lion among the wild animals,
like a young lion prowling among flocks of sheep,
which tramples and tears as it goes, with no one to rescue.
May your hand be raised in triumph over your foes,
and may all your enemies be cut off.

Horses, cities and idols cut off

On that day, declares the LORD,
I will cut off your horses from among you
and destroy your chariots.
I will cut off the cities of your land
and pull down all your strongholds.
I will cut off the sorceries you practice,
and you will have no more fortune-tellers.
I will cut off your carved idols and your sacred stones from among you,
and you will never again bow down to what your own hands have made.
I will uproot your Asherah poles from among you
and destroy your cities.
In anger and fury I will take vengeance
on the nations that have not obeyed.

fields.title: Micah 6
fields.body_html:
The LORD’s case against his people

Listen to what the LORD says:
Stand up, plead your case before the mountains;
let the hills hear your voice.
Hear the case of the LORD, you mountains,
you everlasting foundations of the earth!
For the LORD has a lawsuit against his people;
he will argue it against Israel.
My people, what have I done to you? How have I made you weary?
Testify against me!
For I brought you up out of the land of Egypt;
I redeemed you from the house where you were slaves.
I sent Moses, Aaron, and Miriam
to lead you.
My people, remember what Balak king of Moab plotted,
and how Balaam son of Beor answered him.
Remember the way from Shittim to Gilgal,
so that you may know the saving deeds of the LORD.
“What shall I bring when I come before the LORD
and bow down before God on high?
Shall I come to him with burnt offerings,
with year-old calves?
Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams,
with ten thousand streams of olive oil?
Shall I give my firstborn for my rebellion,
the child of my body for my own sin?”
He has told you, mortal, what is good.
And what does the LORD ask of you except to do justice, to love loyalty,
and to walk humbly with your God?

Wicked scales and false weights

The voice of the LORD calls out to the city,
and the wise will respect your name:
Listen to the rod of punishment, and to the one who appointed it!
Is there still, in the house of the wicked,
treasure gained by wickedness,
and the short measure that is cursed?
Can I be counted pure with dishonest scales
and a bag of false weights?
Her rich are full of violence;
her people speak lies,
and their tongues deceive with every word.
So I in turn will strike you a sickening blow
and bring you to ruin because of your sins.
You will eat, but not be satisfied;
your stomach will still be empty.
You will store things up, but save nothing,
and what you do save I will hand over to the sword.
You will sow, but you will not harvest;
you will press olives, but not rub yourselves with the oil;
you will tread grapes, but not drink the wine.
The decrees of Omri are carefully kept, and all the practices of Ahab’s house,
and you follow their counsels.
So I will make you a horror and your people an object of scorn,
and you will bear the disgrace of my people.

fields.title: Micah 7
fields.body_html:
No one upright is left

Woe is me! I am like one who comes when the summer fruit is gathered,
when the grape harvest has been gleaned:
not a cluster of grapes is left to eat,
not one of the early figs I long for.
The faithful have vanished from the land;
there is not one upright person left.
They all lie in wait to shed blood;
they hunt one another with nets.
Their hands are skilled at doing evil;
the official makes demands,
the judge asks for a bribe,
and the powerful man speaks out what he craves, and together they twist it.
The best of them is like a brier,
the most upright worse than a hedge of thorns.
The day your watchmen warned of has come, the day of your punishment;
now is the time of their confusion.
Do not trust a neighbor;
put no confidence in a friend.
Even with the woman who lies in your arms,
guard the doors of your mouth.
For a son treats his father with contempt,
a daughter rises against her mother,
a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law;
a person’s enemies are the people of their own household.
But I will keep watch for the LORD;
I will put my hope in the God who saves me;
my God will hear me.
Do not gloat over me, my enemy!
I have fallen, but I will rise.
Though I sit in darkness,
the LORD is my light.

The LORD will bring me out into the light

I will bear the anger of the LORD,
because I have sinned against him,
until he takes up my case and wins justice for me.
He will bring me out into the light,
and I will see his righteousness.
Then my enemy will see it,
and shame will cover her,
she who taunted me, “Where is the LORD your God?”
My eyes will watch her downfall;
now she will be trodden down like mud in the streets.
A day is coming for building your walls;
on that day your boundary will be extended far.
On that day people will come to you
from Assyria and the cities of Egypt,
from Egypt as far as the Euphrates,
from sea to sea and from mountain to mountain.
But the earth will become desolate because of those who live in it,
as the result of what they have done.

Who is a God like you?

Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock that belongs to you,
which lives alone
in a forest in the middle of Carmel.
Let them graze in Bashan and Gilead as they did long ago.
As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt,
I will show them wonders.
The nations will see and be ashamed,
for all their power;
they will lay their hands on their mouths;
their ears will be deafened.
They will lick the dust like a serpent,
like creatures that crawl on the ground.
They will come trembling out of their fortresses;
they will turn in dread to the LORD our God
and will be afraid of you.
Who is a God like you, who forgives wrongdoing and passes over rebellion
for the remnant of his inheritance?
He does not keep his anger forever,
because he delights in loyal love.
He will again show us compassion
and trample our wrongdoings underfoot.
You will hurl all their sins into the depths of the sea.
You will show faithfulness to Jacob
and loyal love to Abraham,
as you promised our ancestors on oath long ago.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
You will show faithfulness to Jacob and loyal love to Abraham, as you promised our ancestors on oath long ago.

— Micah 7:20

Micah ends by reaching back to the beginning. The prophet who watched Samaria fall and saw Jerusalem’s ruin coming closes his book with Jacob and Abraham, and with an oath God swore long before any of it. Whatever happens to the cities, the promise stands, because it rests not on the people’s faithfulness but on God’s.

The question the book leaves with you

Micah leaves two questions, and they belong together. The first is ours: “What shall I bring when I come before the LORD?” It is the question of anyone who has felt the weight of their own wrongdoing and wondered what could possibly make it right. Micah’s answer is not more sacrifice but a different life: to do justice, to love loyalty, and to walk humbly with your God. It sounds simple, and it is the work of a lifetime.

The second question is the prophet’s, and it is the answer to the first: “Who is a God like you?” Micah knew that no one keeps the requirements of 6:8 perfectly, not the rulers of Jerusalem and not the prophet himself. So the book ends not with what we bring to God but with what God does with what we bring him: he forgives, he passes over rebellion, he tramples our wrongdoings underfoot and hurls our sins into the sea. Justice, loyalty and humility are the shape of a life lived in response to a God like that.

Where the story goes next

Micah’s warning was heard. Hezekiah repented, and Jerusalem was spared when the Assyrians besieged it. A century later, when the city had forgotten again, Micah’s words saved Jeremiah’s life. And seven centuries later, his promise about Bethlehem was read aloud in Herod’s palace, while a child lay in a house in the village Micah had named, the ruler “whose origins are from of old”, who would shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD and be his people’s peace.

Where to go from here

  • On what the LORD asks (Micah 6:6–8). Alexander Maclaren’s God’s Requirements and God’s Gift, which shows how deep the requirements of 6:8 go and how God’s gift in Christ meets our failure to keep them; and Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s The Good Way of Coming Before the Lord, which answers the question of 6:6 with the way of coming in Christ.
  • On the ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5). Charles H. Spurgeon’s reading for February 27 in Evening by Evening, on the one whose origins are from of old (5:2), and his reading for August 19 in Morning by Morning, on the shepherd-king who stands firm in the strength of the LORD (5:4); and, for children, “The Promise of a Child” in Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets, an Ochorus Original.
  • On the one who breaks through (Micah 2:13). Spurgeon’s reading for August 24 in Morning by Morning.
  • On hope in the dark (Micah 7:7–8). Spurgeon’s readings for January 31 and May 4 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith.
  • On sins thrown into the sea (Micah 7:19). Spurgeon’s reading for December 21 in The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith; and Corrie ten Boom’s talk The Greatest of These Is Love, in which she tells how she learned to forgive and how God casts our confessed sins into the depths of the sea.
  • On the nations streaming to Zion (Micah 4). Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, in the chapter “The conversion of the Gentiles has been predicted by Micah”; and Augustine’s The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 30, on Micah’s mountain and his prophecy of Bethlehem.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Micah in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read Micah again, and let the countryman’s picture of God’s kingdom stay with you, a world where no one takes another’s field and everyone is at home:

Everyone will sit under their own vine and under their own fig tree, with no one to frighten them, for the mouth of the LORD of Armies has spoken.

— Micah 4:4
